newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Don't let the fruitcakes take over NZ, says Bolger.
newsitem.headline: Don't let the fruitcakes take over NZ, says Bolger.

text.p: Prime Minister Jim Bolger delivered what he called a "reality check" to business leaders in Auckland on Wednesday and raised concerns for New Zealand's future under a left-wing government.
Bolger told the Auckland Chamber of Commerce he feared for the future of New Zealand.

More than two weeks ago at the opening in Auckland of the National Party's campaign, he said New Zealand must stay with "the economic recipe. That we must not allow the fruitcakes to take over the kitchen.
"I said that then and repeat it today because I fear that all that we have sacrificed, all that we have worked for, all that is so close, could all be lost in just 10 days' time."
Bolger said that Labour was polling at about half the support it had in 1993 and would not be able to form a government by itself.
Nor could it form a government with the help of New Zealand First alone.
"Labour can only hope to lead a government with the active involvement and support of the Alliance."

He said the Alliance's "extreme economics and social policies" should be studied, because these would have to be accommodated by Labour leader Helen Clark if she were to achieve her ambition and lead the next government.

Bolger said the Alliance would demand: replacement of the Employment Contracts Act with legislation that would again give unions the "whip hand"; the repeal of GST and its replacement with the old social credit financial transaction tax; and a progressive tax system that would see massive increases in personal taxes.

For instance, he said that in the income range of $24,000 to $30,000 from next July under National, taxpayers would pay 21 cents in the dollar. With Alliance, that figure would be 35 cents in the dollar.
In the income range $35,000 to $38,000, the difference would be 21 cents under National and 41 cents under Alliance policy.
"Those massive tax increases are necessary to fund the Alliance's massive spending promises of almost $15 billion extra between 1996-97 and 1998-99," Bolger said.
Bolger said anyone foolish enough to believe that a Labour-led NZ First, Alliance coalition would have no cost to them was wrong.
